Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies, Indigenous Peoples' representatives, participants, ladies and gentlemen. Let me first express my gratitude to everyone who responded to my call for contribution. to my two reports that I'm presenting today. As we commence the celebration of the 20th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, my report on violations committed against Indigenous women's and girls' reproductive rights reviews how States have so far addressed these violations and seek to remind those States that the end of the declaration cannot be achieved without first addressing those historical injustices. Upholding sexual and reproductive rights of Indigenous women is essential to the survival, continuity and self-determination of Indigenous peoples. Indigenous women are life givers, knowledge holders, caregivers and transmitters of languages, cultures, and identities. And because of the central role that Indigenous women play, their bodies and reproductive capability have historically been and continue to be the second primary target after Indigenous Peoples' land for those seeking to eradicate Indigenous Peoples as distinct nation, peoples, and identities. Forced sterilization or contraception, the enforcement of mandatory boarding school rife with sexual violence, the demonization or outright criminalization of Indigenous midwifery practice, and severe acts of sexual violence aimed at instilling fear in an entire community exemplify the historical violations of Indigenous women reproductive rights and persisted for decades across regions and countries. The driver of these violations were multiples, including colonialism, systemic racism, patriarchies, and effort to assimilate or erase Indigenous peoples as cultural nations. These forces intersected to create an environment in which Indigenous women and girls were primarily targets, abused and ill-treated. The report also highlights a variety of contemporary drivers of these violations. One of these drivers is militarization, which frequently lead to increased violence and instability within Indigenous people communities. Environmental pollution is another key drivers. The reproductive right and health, as well as well-being of Indigenous women and girls are impacted by the contamination of land, water, air, including by extractive industries. Armed conflicts are also a cause that exacerbates the vulnerability of Indigenous women and girls to sexual violence and exploitation. The report further revealed that in many cases, conservation initiatives have also resulted in violations of reproductive rights of Indigenous women and girls. The legacy of these historical injustices remain visible today. Indigenous women and girls continue to experience disproportionately high level of sexual violence, trafficking, reproductive coercion, maternal mortality, forced separation from their children, criminalization of traditional health practices, and significant barriers to accessing culturally appropriate health care. The report notes that in recent decades, some states have addressed some of these violations of Indigenous women's and girl reproductive rights, but responses remain sporadic, uneven, and partial. So far, the main efforts of redress have included elements of public apology, national inquiries or hearings, truth-telling initiatives, reparation measures, including some compensation. However, only a small number of States have implemented the full range of redress measures, which include legal and policy reforms, guarantee of non-repetition, and full judicial remedies. For States to achieve genuine reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples, as provided for by the Declaration, it is imperative that they comprehensively redress both this historical and contemporary form of violation of Indigenous women and girl reproductive rights. This entails recognizing past and present injustices, providing reparations, implementing definitive action to avert future violation and assuring accountability. Truth telling, repression and institutional reform must be central on centered on the women affected and carried out in a manner that avoid repetition. The report makes nimrus key actionable recommendation to states and other stakeholders, including urging states to implement prompt and effective actions to cease these violations, offer reparations to impacted individuals and communities, and establish intercultural health programs and facilities.
